challenges.name: capacity-estimates-quiz
challenges.title: Little's Law and the exam-day peak
challenges.description: Two estimates from the CodeDev capacity plan, checked against the grader metrics of the last exam: how long a backlog takes to drain, and whether daily averages can size the grader fleet.

questions.question:
Grader dashboard, exam day, deadline 10:00:00:

  grader_slots_busy            40 / 40   (09:59 - 10:37)
  grader_jobs_completed_rate   8.9 jobs/s
  grader_job_duration_seconds  mean 4.5 s
  submission_queue_depth       19,870 at 10:00:00, then falling
  POST /submissions rate       near 0 after 10:01 (exam closed)

Statement: "At this throughput the 19,870 queued jobs need about 37 more minutes to drain, which matches results for 10:00 submissions arriving around 10:38."
questions.explanation: True. 40 busy slots with a mean job time of 4.5 s give a throughput of 40 / 4.5 = 8.9 jobs/s (Little's Law: jobs in progress = throughput x time per job, here 40 = 8.9 x 4.5). With no new arrivals the backlog shrinks at the full service rate: 19,870 / 8.9 = 2,233 s, about 37 minutes, so the last of them finishes around 10:38, what the dashboard shows; that comparison is how an estimate is checked against metrics. The misconception is that a queue drains as fast as it filled; it drains at the service rate minus the arrival rate, which during the exam is negative (the queue grows).

questions.question:
Capacity plan, draft:

  daily active learners          20,000
  submissions per active learner  5 / day
  submissions per day            100,000  ->  100,000 / 86,400 s = 1.2 submissions/s
  grader capacity (40 slots, 4.5 s mean)  8.9 jobs/s
  conclusion: "7x headroom, no scaling needed for exam day"

Last exam: 20,400 submissions in the minute before the deadline.

Statement: "Since the daily average is 1.2 submissions/s and the fleet handles 8.9/s, the 40-slot fleet keeps the queue short on exam day."
questions.explanation: False. The daily average spreads 100,000 submissions evenly over 24 hours, but load arrives in bursts: the last exam put 20,400 submissions into one minute, 340/s, about 280 times the average. At 8.9 jobs/s the fleet finishes about 530 of them in that minute and the rest, about 19,900, wait in the queue. Little's Law sizes the fleet for the peak: 340/s x 4.5 s = about 1,530 jobs in progress to keep up, or a smaller fleet plus an agreed drain time (R2c: results within 5 minutes). The misconception is sizing for the average; capacity planning needs the peak rate and how long the peak lasts.
